clinicalPearls: Megaloblastic anemias share a defect in DNA synthesis affecting rapidly dividing marrow cells, producing characteristic morphology with a hypercellular marrow and ineffective erythropoiesis (Harrison 22e p.780).

The usual cause is deficiency of cobalamin (vitamin B12) or folate, but the picture can also arise from genetic or acquired abnormalities of their metabolism or from DNA-synthesis defects unrelated to either vitamin (Harrison 22e p.780).

Body cobalamin stores (about 2-3 mg) are large enough to last 3-4 years if intake stops, whereas folate stores (about 10 mg total, mostly hepatic) suffice for only 3-4 months, so severe folate deficiency can develop rapidly (Harrison 22e p.780, p.781).
Cobalamin is made only by microorganisms; the sole human source is animal-derived food, so strict vegans are at risk of dietary deficiency (Harrison 22e p.781, p.786).

Pernicious anemia, the dominant cause of severe cobalamin deficiency in Western countries, is gastric atrophy with severe lack of intrinsic factor; median onset is age 70-80, it clusters with other organ-specific autoimmune diseases (thyroid disease, vitiligo, type 1 diabetes, Addison disease), and gastric output of acid, pepsin, and intrinsic factor is severely reduced with raised serum gastrin and low pepsinogen I (Harrison 22e p.785, p.786).

Cobalamin deficiency can cause neurologic disease (subacute combined degeneration) with demyelination of posterior and lateral spinal columns, peripheral neuropathy, optic atrophy, and cerebral changes including dementia and psychosis; patients (more often male) present with paresthesias, weakness, or gait difficulty, often with positive Romberg and Lhermitte signs (Harrison 22e p.783).

Peripheral blood shows oval macrocytes with marked aniso-poikilocytosis, an MCV usually >100 fL (unless coexisting microcytosis), and hypersegmented neutrophils (more than five nuclear lobes) (Harrison 22e p.784).

In a nonanemic patient, a few macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils may be the only clue to underlying deficiency, and serum cobalamin may be borderline; supporting tests include MMA, IF/parietal-cell antibodies, and serum gastrin (Harrison 22e p.783, p.784).

Periconceptional folic acid reduces neural tube defects (anencephaly, meningomyelocele, encephalocele, spina bifida) by roughly 80%; the lower the maternal folate, the greater the fetal risk (Harrison 22e p.783).

Older patients with iron deficiency should also be assessed for cobalamin deficiency and vice versa, since coexistence is common (15-20% over age 60) and iron deficiency may blunt the macrocytosis (Harrison 22e p.789).

Removal of 1.2 m or more of terminal ileum, total gastrectomy, fish tapeworm (Diphyllobothrium latum) infestation, and intestinal stagnant-loop syndrome are recognized malabsorptive causes of cobalamin deficiency (Harrison 22e p.786, p.787).
harrison.pathophysiology: The common defect is impaired DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells. In folate or cobalamin deficiency, conversion of deoxyuridine monophosphate (dUMP) to deoxythymidine monophosphate (dTMP) fails because the folate coenzyme 5,10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate, needed for this step, becomes scarce. The shortage of dTTP precursor slows DNA replication, leaving single-stranded breaks; an alternative theory invokes misincorporation of uracil into DNA. Cobalamin is a cofactor for two reactions: methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and the methionine-synthase-mediated methylation of homocysteine to methionine, which also requires 5-methyl-THF. In cobalamin deficiency, 5-methyl-THF accumulates in plasma while intracellular THF (the substrate for folate polyglutamate formation) falls — the methylfolate trap (THF starvation) — explaining high serum folate but low cell folate, and why the anemia of cobalamin deficiency can respond to large folic acid doses. Death of nucleated red cells in the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis) produces unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, raised LDH, raised urine urobilinogen, and reduced haptoglobins (Harrison 22e p.782, p.783, p.785).
additionalDifferentials: Megaloblastic anemia from antifolate/antimetabolite drugs (methotrexate, pyrimethamine, trimethoprim; hydroxyurea, cytarabine, mercaptopurine, thioguanine, AZT) (Harrison 22e p.780, p.790)
Orotic aciduria (responds to uridine) (Harrison 22e p.780, p.790)
Thiamine-responsive megaloblastic anemia (SLC19A2 transporter defect; may have diabetes, deafness, ringed sideroblasts) (Harrison 22e p.780, p.790)
Megaloblastic changes in acute myeloid leukemia and myelodysplasia (refractory to folate/cobalamin) (Harrison 22e p.780, p.790)
Macrocytosis without true megaloblastic change: alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, pregnancy, myelodysplasia, myeloma/paraproteinemia, aplastic anemia, smoking (Harrison 22e p.790)
nonInfectiousMimics: Myelodysplasia (megaloblastoid marrow may mimic megaloblastic anemia and, in severe cases, accumulation of blasts may mimic acute myeloid leukemia) (Harrison 22e p.785)
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (a weakly positive direct antiglobulin test due to complement from ineffective erythropoiesis can lead to a false diagnosis) (Harrison 22e p.785)
Other causes of macrocytosis: alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, pregnancy (Harrison 22e p.790)
additionalInvestigations: Serum cobalamin (ELISA or competitive-binding luminescence assay); note IF antibodies can cause falsely normal results in up to 50% of pernicious anemia cases (Harrison 22e p.788)
Serum methylmalonic acid (raised in cobalamin deficiency sufficient for anemia/neuropathy; fluctuates in renal failure) (Harrison 22e p.788, p.789)
Serum homocysteine (raised in early cobalamin and folate deficiency but nonspecific) (Harrison 22e p.789)
Serum folate and red cell folate (red cell folate reflects body stores; false-normal after transfusion or with high reticulocytes) (Harrison 22e p.789)
Serum gastrin (raised in pernicious anemia) and pepsinogen I (low) (Harrison 22e p.785, p.789)
Intrinsic factor and parietal cell antibodies; gastric endoscopy/biopsy (Harrison 22e p.786, p.789)
Bone marrow examination in selected severely anemic patients (Harrison 22e p.784)
Transglutaminase antibodies to exclude gluten-induced enteropathy in folate deficiency (Harrison 22e p.789)
redFlags: Neurologic signs of subacute combined degeneration: loss of proprioception/vibration, positive Romberg and Lhermitte signs, ataxic/spastic gait, hyperreflexia (Harrison 22e p.783)
Cerebral involvement: dementia, depression, psychosis, cognitive impairment, visual impairment from optic atrophy (Harrison 22e p.783)
Nonanemic patient with neurologic/psychiatric features and low or borderline serum cobalamin (deficiency must be actively confirmed) (Harrison 22e p.783)
Severe thrombocytopenia (rarely <40 x 10^9/L) with bruising (Harrison 22e p.783, p.784)
Marked marrow blast accumulation in severe cases mimicking acute leukemia (Harrison 22e p.785)
harrison.prognosis: With regular treatment of pernicious anemia, life expectancy is normal in women; men historically had slightly reduced life expectancy due to a higher incidence of gastric carcinoma, with current data unavailable. Neurologic recovery depends on duration before treatment, and a therapeutic trial of at least 3 months may be needed to judge improvement in neuropsychiatric cases. Untreated severe deficiency causes progressive anemia, neurologic deterioration, and infertility (Harrison 22e p.783, p.786).
pitfalls: Intrinsic-factor antibodies can produce falsely normal serum cobalamin in up to 50% of pernicious anemia patients tested by certain assays — a normal level does not exclude pernicious anemia when clinical suspicion is strong (Harrison 22e p.788).
Giving large doses of folic acid before excluding/correcting cobalamin deficiency can allow cobalamin neuropathy to progress despite hematologic response (Harrison 22e p.789, p.790).
Serum folate falls with recent poor diet but rises in severe cobalamin deficiency (methylfolate trap) and in stagnant-loop syndrome, so it can mislead (Harrison 22e p.789).
Mildly elevated MMA and/or homocysteine occur in up to 30% of healthy volunteers and in 15% of elderly with normal cobalamin, so cutoffs and clinical significance are uncertain (Harrison 22e p.789).
Coexisting iron deficiency may mask macrocytosis; the term 'megaloblastoid' is best avoided as it refers to myelodysplastic change refractory to vitamin therapy (Harrison 22e p.785, p.789).
A weakly positive direct antiglobulin test from ineffective erythropoiesis can be misread as autoimmune hemolytic anemia (Harrison 22e p.785).
harrison.severityClassification: Severity is gauged by the degree of anemia and parallels the morphologic changes; marrow involvement is described as severe, intermediate, mild, or early. In megaloblastic anemia due to cobalamin deficiency the serum cobalamin is usually <74 pmol/L (100 ng/L), with 74-148 pmol/L (100-200 ng/L) regarded as borderline; the more severe the deficiency, the lower the level, and very low levels occur with spinal cord involvement even without anemia (Harrison 22e p.785, p.788).
